etymology: One of the cities of the plain of Jordan, overthrown with Sodom and Gomorrah; the name means “earth” or “red ground.”
biblical_def: Admah was one of the cities of the plain of Jordan, listed with Sodom, Gomorrah, and Zeboiim among the confederacy smitten in Abraham’s day: “these made war with Bera king of Sodom…Shinab king of Admah, and Shemeber king of Zeboiim” (Gen 14:2). It shared the guilt of those cities, and it shared their doom. When the LORD rained fire and brimstone upon Sodom, Admah too was consumed, so that Moses names it as a byword of judgment: the land “is brimstone, and salt, and burning…like the overthrow of Sodom, and Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboim, which the LORD overthrew in his anger, and in his wrath” (Deu 29:23). Yet the name of Admah returns once more, in one of the most tender passages of the prophets, where God pleads over backsliding Israel: “How shall I make thee as Admah? how shall I set thee as Zeboim? mine heart is turned within me, my repentings are kindled together” (Hos 11:8). So Admah, the very emblem of deserved destruction, becomes the measure of God’s astonishing mercy: He will not deal with His covenant people as He dealt with the cities of the plain, for His heart is moved with pity toward them. The believer sees in Admah both the certain judgment his sins deserved and the grace that spared him, turning away the wrath he had earned, and setting him not as Admah, but as a son.

etymology: One of the cities of the plain of Jordan, overthrown with Sodom and Gomorrah; spelled Zeboim in Deuteronomy and Hosea. The name is taken to mean “gazelles” or “wild beasts.” Not to be confounded with the valley of Zeboim near Michmash.
biblical_def: Zeboiim was one of the cities of the plain of Jordan, joined with Sodom, Gomorrah, and Admah in guilt and in doom. Its king Shemeber fought in the confederacy of the plain: “these made war with Bera king of Sodom…and Shemeber king of Zeboiim” (Gen 14:2). The plain of Jordan was once well watered everywhere, “even as the garden of the LORD” (Gen 13:10), and Lot chose it for its beauty and fatness, pitching his tent toward Sodom — a choice made by the eye and not by faith, that ended in the fire. For when the wickedness of the cities was full, the LORD overthrew them all in His anger, Zeboiim with the rest, so that the fruitful plain became brimstone and salt (Deu 29:23). Yet, like Admah, Zeboiim is named again in Hosea’s tender plea, where God’s mercy overrides the judgment His people deserve: “how shall I set thee as Zeboim? mine heart is turned within me” (Hos 11:8). Zeboiim thus stands as a double warning and comfort: a warning that the fairest earthly prospect, chosen by the covetous eye apart from God, may end in ruin; and a comfort that the LORD, though He justly destroyed the cities of the plain, will not so destroy the people on whom His heart is set.

etymology: A valley in the territory of Benjamin, near Michmash, looking toward the wilderness; the name means “valley of hyenas” or “of wild beasts.” Not to be confounded with Zeboiim, the city of the plain.
biblical_def: The valley of Zeboim is a ravine in the land of Benjamin, near Michmash, looking down toward the wilderness of Jordan. It is named in the account of Israel’s low estate under the Philistines, when the raiders of the enemy ranged the land in three companies: “another company turned to the way of the border that looketh to the valley of Zeboim toward the wilderness” (1Sa 13:18). Those were bitter days: the Philistines had so mastered and disarmed Israel that no smith was left, and in the day of battle “there was neither sword nor spear found in the hand of any of the people” (1Sa 13:22), save with Saul and Jonathan alone. The people of God were oppressed, plundered, and defenceless, hiding in caves and pits, chastened for their sins. Yet the very next chapter breaks with deliverance, when Jonathan and his armour-bearer, trusting that there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few, went up against the garrison and God wrought a great victory. So the valley of Zeboim, a place of the enemy’s raiding, stands at the low point before the LORD’s deliverance. It teaches that God may let His people be brought very low, disarmed and afflicted, and yet is never restrained from saving; the darkest hour of oppression is often the eve of His salvation.

etymology: The chief stronghold of Edom, an ancient royal city; the name means “fortress” or “sheepfold.” In Isaiah, the place from which the mighty Redeemer comes with dyed garments.
biblical_def: Bozrah was the chief stronghold of Edom, an ancient royal city of that land: “Bela died, and Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his stead” (Gen 36:33). Its name means fortress or sheepfold. Because Edom, the seed of Esau, was the perpetual and bitter enemy of Israel, Bozrah became in the prophets a figure of the nations under the judgment of God: “the LORD hath a sacrifice in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Idumea” (Isa 34:6). But it is Isaiah 63 that lifts Bozrah to its greatest height, in a vision of the Messiah returning victorious from the slaughter of His enemies: “Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? this that is glorious in his apparel, travelling in the greatness of his strength? I that speak in righteousness, mighty to save” (Isa 63:1). He answers that He has trodden the winepress alone, and of the people there was none with Him (Isa 63:3); His garments are stained not with His own toil only but with the blood of the enemies He has trampled in His fury. So Bozrah becomes the backdrop for one of Scripture’s grandest portraits of Christ: the lone, mighty Redeemer, glorious in apparel, treading down the foes of His people in the day of vengeance, and coming forth mighty to save. He who was once trodden for us now treads His enemies, and none can stand before Him.

etymology: A region and city of Edom, famed of old for its wise men; the name means “south” or “the south country.” Named for Teman, a grandson of Esau, but here the land itself, not the man.
biblical_def: Teman was a region and city of Edom, in the south country, famed throughout the ancient world for the wisdom of its men. Eliphaz, the first and gravest of Job’s comforters, was “Eliphaz the Temanite” (Job 2:11), a man of much worldly wisdom who yet spoke wrongly of God. When the LORD pronounced judgment upon Edom, He struck at this very glory: “Is wisdom no more in Teman? is counsel perished from the prudent? is their wisdom vanished?” (Jer 49:7). The famed wisdom of Teman, being the wisdom of a proud and God-defying people, was to be confounded and brought to nothing. Yet in one glorious verse Teman is given a nobler use, as the prophet pictures the coming of God in majesty: “God came from Teman, and the Holy One from mount Paran…His glory covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise” (Hab 3:3). So Teman holds together the whole judgment of Scripture upon human wisdom: the boasted wisdom of the world, even at its famed height, perishes and is confounded before God; but the wisdom that comes down from above, the wisdom of God Himself, fills the heavens with glory. “Where is the wise?” asks the apostle; “hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?” The believer forsakes the wisdom of Teman for Christ, who is made unto us wisdom from God.

etymology: A fortified city in the far north of Israel, in the territory of Naphtali; the name means “meadow of the house of Maachah.” Famed for the wise woman who saved it in the days of David.
biblical_def: Abel-beth-maachah was a fortified city in the far north of Israel, in the land of Naphtali. Its most memorable hour came in the revolt of Sheba against David, when Sheba fled there and Joab besieged the city, casting up a mound and battering the wall to bring it down. Then a wise woman of the city cried out over the wall to Joab: “Hear, hear; say, I pray you, unto Joab, Come near hither, that I may speak with thee” (2Sa 20:16). She pleaded for the city with weighty words: “I am one of them that are peaceable and faithful in Israel: thou seekest to destroy a city and a mother in Israel: why wilt thou swallow up the inheritance of the LORD?” (2Sa 20:19). Learning that only the one rebel Sheba was sought, she counselled the men of the city to deliver up his head, and so by her wisdom the whole city was spared and the siege lifted. This was a city esteemed a “mother in Israel,” a place of settled peace and faithfulness. Yet its faithfulness did not exempt it from the sorrows of the northern border: Ben-hadad of Syria smote it (1Ki 15:20), and long after, Tiglath-pileser of Assyria carried its people captive. Abel-beth-maachah preaches the honor of peaceable faithfulness and the worth of one wise soul who, seeking the good of the whole, may turn away destruction with a word.

etymology: A town on the border of Zebulun, the birthplace of the prophet Jonah; called Gittah-hepher in Joshua. The name means “winepress of digging” or “winepress of the well.” Not to be confounded with Gath of the Philistines.
biblical_def: Gath-hepher was a town on the border of Zebulun, in lower Galilee, named in the marking of that tribe’s bounds as Gittah-hepher (Jos 19:13). Its lasting fame is as the birthplace of the prophet Jonah. When Jeroboam the second restored the coasts of Israel, it was “according to the word of the LORD God of Israel, which he spake by the hand of his servant Jonah, the son of Amittai, the prophet, which was of Gathhepher” (2Ki 14:25). From this obscure Galilean town came the reluctant prophet whom God sent to Nineveh, the great Gentile city, and whose flight, storm, and three days in the fish became the very sign our Lord took for His own death and resurrection: “as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale’s belly; so shall the Son of man be”. Gath-hepher rebukes, in passing, the later Pharisees who scorned Galilee, saying, “out of Galilee ariseth no prophet” — for out of Galilean Gath-hepher had come Jonah of old. And the story of its prophet preaches the sovereign, surprising mercy of God, who would spare repentant Nineveh though His prophet grudged it, teaching that the LORD’s compassion reaches even to the great and wicked cities of the nations, and that He will have mercy on whom He will have mercy.
webster_summary: A town of Zebulun in Galilee, the birthplace of the prophet Jonah; a witness to God’s surprising mercy to the nations. Distinct from Gath of the Philistines.

etymology: A valley on the border of Judah and Philistia where Delilah dwelt, in whose snare Samson was undone; the name means “choice vine” or “a vine of choice grapes.”
biblical_def: The valley of Sorek was a fertile vale on the border between Judah and the Philistine plain, remembered as the place of Samson’s fatal love: “it came to pass afterward, that he loved a woman in the valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah” (Jdg 16:4). The name means choice vine, and the vale was doubtless a place of vineyards; but its choicest fruit, in the story, was a bitter one. Here the mightiest of the judges, whom no army could bind and no gate could hold, was undone not by force but by unlawful love. Delilah wearied him with her daily pressing until he told her the secret of his strength; and when his locks were shorn, “he wist not that the LORD was departed from him” (Jdg 16:20). The strong man was made weak, his eyes were put out, and he ground at the mill of his enemies. The valley of Sorek is thus one of Scripture’s sharpest warnings against the snare of illicit desire: “For she hath cast down many wounded: yea, many strong men have been slain by her” (Pro 7:26). No strength of body, no gift, no calling is proof against the seductions of the flesh when a man dallies with temptation and grieves the Spirit. The vine of Sorek looked fair, but its wine was death; and the believer is warned to flee, not to flirt with, the sin that so easily besets.

etymology: A valley or brook near Hebron whence the spies brought the great cluster of grapes; the name means “cluster.” Also the name of an Amorite ally of Abraham. Here chiefly the valley of the cluster.
biblical_def: The brook, or valley, of Eshcol lay near Hebron, and gave the spies of Israel their proof of the goodness of the promised land. When Moses sent twelve men to search out Canaan, “they came unto the brook of Eshcol, and cut down from thence a branch with one cluster of grapes, and they bare it between two upon a staff” (Num 13:23), so great was the fruit; “the place was called the brook Eshcol, because of the cluster of grapes which the children of Israel cut down from thence” (Num 13:24). The name means cluster. That single bunch was a pledge and foretaste of the good land flowing with milk and honey. Yet the very men who carried the cluster brought back an evil report: they magnified the giants and the walled cities, “a land that eateth up the inhabitants thereof” (Num 13:32), and by their unbelief they turned the hearts of the people to despair, so that a whole generation perished in the wilderness. Only Caleb and Joshua believed God’s promise; “my servant Caleb…had another spirit with him, and hath followed me fully” (Num 14:24). So the valley of Eshcol holds together the goodness of God’s promise and the wickedness of unbelief: the cluster in the hand and the giants in the eye. The believer is warned not to let the giants outweigh the grapes, but to reckon, with Caleb, that the God who promised is able to perform, and to enter His rest by faith.

etymology: A city of Mesopotamia, by the river Euphrates, the home of Balaam the son of Beor, the hireling prophet whom Balak sent for to curse Israel; the name is taken to mean “interpreter of dreams” or “soothsaying.”
biblical_def: Pethor was a city of Mesopotamia, by the river Euphrates, the home of Balaam the son of Beor. When Balak king of Moab feared the advancing hosts of Israel, “he sent messengers therefore unto Balaam the son of Beor to Pethor, which is by the river of the land of the children of his people, to call him” (Num 22:5), to come and curse Israel for reward. Balaam was a soothsayer who knew something of the true God, yet loved the wages of unrighteousness; and the whole account is a monument to the sovereignty of God over the tongues and schemes of men. Though Balaam came coveting the curse-money, God would not suffer him to curse: “the LORD thy God would not hearken unto Balaam; but the LORD thy God turned the curse into a blessing unto thee, because the LORD thy God loved thee” (Deu 23:5). Four times Balaam opened his mouth to curse, and four times God turned it to blessing. Yet Balaam, unable to curse, taught Balak the darker counsel of seducing Israel to sin at Baal-peor, and so is forever branded for “the way of Balaam…who loved the wages of unrighteousness” and for the doctrine that casts a stumblingblock before God’s people. Pethor thus stands for the covetous hireling in religion, whom God overrules for His people’s good even while judging his greed; no curse can light on those whom God has blessed.

corruption_summary: A city of Scripture whose prophet embodies covetous, hireling religion; it recovers the truth that God turns the curse into blessing and no curse can light on His people.
corruption_paragraphs: Pethor and its prophet name a live and abiding corruption: the way of Balaam, the covetous hireling in religion who loves the wages of unrighteousness, and who, unable to curse God’s people outright, seeks to seduce them into sin. His doctrine, casting a stumblingblock before the saints, is warned against to the very churches of Revelation.

Yet the deeper truth of Pethor is the sovereignty of God over every curse and scheme. He would not suffer Balaam to curse, but turned the curse into a blessing, because He loved His people. No enchantment prospers against Jacob, no divination against Israel; and the believer rests in a God who overrules the greed and malice of men, so that no curse can finally light upon those whom He has blessed in Christ.
